title: Proof pages for a manufacturer
metaTitle: What a manufacturer case study must show
excerpt: A useful proof names the constraint, the decision, and how the object was made. End with how a similar buyer can talk to sales or download a spec.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band, for a piece on reading a job the way a buyer would.
caption: Two people reading one screen together. A proof should be that inspectable. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs at the start of a manufacturer case study?
faqs.answer: The constraint. A tolerance, a material, a volume, or a document the job had to satisfy. A peer should recognize the bind, and a customer secret should stay out. If the job was routine, it may belong on the services page instead.

faqs.question: Which numbers are safe to publish?
faqs.answer: Numbers you can source and that the customer allows. A scrap result on the characteristic you were asked to fix, a quantity, or a lead time from approved file to first shipment. Leave out anything you could not show an engineer who asked to see the record.

faqs.question: How should the case study end?
faqs.answer: With a next step for a similar buyer. Talk to sales or download the spec for that process, and say what to include. Also say who the story is a poor analogy for, so the page does not invite work you will decline.

markdown:
A manufacturer case study page should show a buyer who needs specs and confidence three things: the constraint, the decision, and the object and how it was made. Screenshots of a factory, or a gallery of finished parts with no decision attached, are decoration. The page ends by telling a similar buyer how to talk to sales or download a spec.

Write it as a record of judgment. What was hard, what you chose, what left the building. A reader who makes parts for a living can feel the difference between a job that happened and a mood board with a logo on it.

## Open on the constraint

The first sentences name the bind. A tolerance the previous process could not hold. A material that moved during finishing. A volume too small for the buyer's usual supplier and too demanding for a prototype shop. A documentation pack their quality team would not waive. The constraint should be specific enough that a peer would recognize it.

Keep the customer's secrets where you promised to. You can describe the constraint without publishing their drawing, their annual volume, or their unreleased product. "A die-cast housing for outdoor electronics, with a flatness callout the as-cast part could not meet" is often enough. Ask the customer what may be public before you draft. A proof page that burns a relationship is not a marketing asset.

Name the industry or the product type only as far as it helps the next buyer see themselves. A pile of sector nouns in the opening is a costume. One clear situation is stronger. The reader should think, within a few lines, that this job is a cousin of theirs or that it is not. Both outcomes are useful. The wrong buyer leaving early saves everyone a call.

Set the stakes in operational language. Scrap, a missed build, a field failure, a line-down risk, a cosmetic standard a retailer would reject. You do not need a dramatic story. You need the reason the job was not routine. If the job was routine, it may not deserve a proof page. Routine excellence can live as a sentence on the services page.

## Show the decision, including what you ruled out

The middle of the page is the decision. What you changed, what you refused to change, and why. Added a machining pass after the casting. Switched a weld sequence. Built a fixture so a short run could still be repeatable. Told the buyer the finish they asked for would fail the environment, and agreed a different one.

Include a path you did not take, when you can say it plainly. The point is judgment. A buyer who needs confidence is looking for evidence that someone weighed options. A page that only lists activities, cut, washed, packed, reads like a traveler. A page that says why this route and not a cheaper one reads like a supplier.

Attribute the decision to a role. Process engineering, quality, the founder, the cell lead. You do not need a hero narrative. You need an owner. Unowned decisions feel invented. If the customer made the decisive call and you executed it, say that. Honesty about who decided is part of the proof.

Keep the technical detail at the level a visiting engineer can follow. One figure, one process note, one sentence of consequence. A dump of every parameter will lose the commercial reader, and it may give away more than the customer allowed. Link the public spec for the general process. Keep the job-specific numbers inside what you have permission to show.

## The object, and how it was made

Show the object. A photograph with scale, a before-and-after of the feature that was hard, or a still of the setup that made the decision real. The picture is evidence. A beauty shot with the problem cropped out fails the page even if the lighting is good.

Then show how it was made, in the sequence that mattered. You do not retell the entire plant tour. You retell the steps that answered the constraint. Incoming material check, the operation you added, the inspection that proved the result, the pack that protected the feature in transit. Four beats are enough.

If a standard, a certificate, or a first-article document was part of the close, say what it covered. "First-article report on the three characteristics the customer marked critical" is a fact. "Full quality documentation provided" is a fog machine. Use the fact.

Numbers belong when they are yours to publish and they describe the job. A scrap rate on the characteristic you were asked to fix. A lead time from approved file to first shipment. A quantity. Leave out numbers you cannot source, and leave out numbers the customer considers confidential even if they flatter you. A proof page with an invented improvement is a liability the first time a buyer asks to see the report.

## Write it so a peer can audit the story

Use the customer's words for the requirement and your words for the method. Quote a requirement only when you have a clean, approved line to quote. Paraphrase the rest. The voice of the page should match the rest of the site: plain, specific, free of victory laps.

Structure the page in the same order every time, so a buyer reading a second proof knows where to look. Constraint. Decision. Making. Result. How to start a similar conversation. Predictable structure is a kindness. It is also how a small marketing team keeps the next proof from drifting into a press release.

[Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for first-hand experience and for pages that leave a reader clearer about what to do. A case study meets that standard when the constraint is real, the decision is owned, and the next step is obvious. It misses when the page could have been written without anyone walking the floor.

Give the page a specific title. The object and the constraint, not "Case study" and not "Success story." The browser title can be a touch more explicit about the process. One main heading. The rest of the page supports it. Several slogans at the top force the reader to guess which sentence is the point.

## End on a similar buyer's next step

The last section is for the person who sees their own job in the story. Tell them how to start. Talk to sales, or download the spec that covers this process. Say what to include: a drawing, the characteristic that is hard, the volume, the date. Match the action used on the homepage and the services page. A proof page with a unique, longer form punishes the reader who was ready.

Say who the proof is a good analogy for, and who it is not. "Relevant if you have a cast part that needs a machined sealing face." "Less relevant if you need a production die and a million-piece run." That boundary continues the honesty of the case. It also protects sales from a wave of mismatched inquiries the story accidentally invited.

If the customer may be named, use the name once, clearly, with permission. If they may not, do not hint with a riddle of details that identifies them anyway. Anonymity is a straight decision. Half-anonymity is how trust breaks on both sides.

Link one related spec and, if you have it, one related service block. The proof should connect back into the offer. A beautiful story that dead-ends in "thanks for reading" wastes the confidence it just earned.

## What to leave out

Leave out the factory cliché. The ribbon cutting, the aerial, the lobby. Leave out awards that did not touch this job. Leave out a stack of logos in the header that have nothing to do with the constraint. Leave out timelines you cannot explain if someone asks for the underlying record.

Leave out screenshots of internal software unless the decision was about information, and even then crop to the decision. A full ERP screen is usually unreadable and usually confidential. A sentence will do. The instruction from the work itself is simple. A picture without a decision is decoration, so every picture on this page has to be able to answer "what choice does this show?"

Do not publish a proof you would be unwilling to discuss with an engineer for fifteen minutes. The page will attract exactly that conversation. If the answer to a likely question is "we cannot talk about that," choose a different job or a coarser level of detail before you publish.

## How a small set stays honest

Three strong proofs beat twelve thin ones. Choose jobs that cover the offers you want more of. If you want more finishing work, at least one proof should turn on finishing. If the set is all prototype heroics and your business is repeat production, the set is advertising a company you are not.

Date the page or show the period of the work. Processes change. A proof from a cell you have since rebuilt should say so, or it should come down. A short note at the top, "shipped 2024, process still in use," keeps the library trustworthy. Someone on the team owns that review. It can be the same person who owns the spec revisions.

On a Hanabi project, proof is treated as a piece of the site, with the same type, the same action, and a place in the portal for the permissions and the source photos. The studio designs and builds the page. You keep the right to say what may be shown. That split matters, because the customer relationship is yours.

If you want help turning a real job into a page a buyer can use, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the constraint, the decision, and what you are allowed to show. The draft should be able to survive a conversation with your own process engineer.

The reader who believes the proof still has to find the rest of the offer without learning your org chart.
